title: Field-Level Optimistic Concurrency
prompt: An inventory API uses optimistic concurrency, but instead of rejecting every stale write it merges edits to different fields. Each `Row(Id, Version, Title, Quantity)` starts with both fields last changed at its current `Version`. Apply each `Update(Id, ExpectedVersion, Title?, Quantity?)` in order (a `null` field means 'not changing it') and record one outcome string per update: `"{Id}: not found"` if the row does not exist; `"{Id}: invalid version {ExpectedVersion}"` if the client claims a version newer than the row's; `"{Id}: no changes"` if both fields are null; `"{Id}: conflict on Title, Quantity"` (listing only the offending fields, Title first) if any field it touches was changed after `ExpectedVersion`, in which case nothing from that update is applied; otherwise apply the fields, bump `Version` by one, note which fields changed at the new version, and record `"{Id}: applied v{Version}"`. Return `MergeResult(Outcomes, Rows)` with rows in their original order.

explanation.beginner: Optimistic concurrency means: every row carries a version number, a client says 'I read version 3', and the server refuses the write if someone else changed the row since then. That stops lost updates, but it also refuses harmless cases, like one person renaming a product while another changes its stock. Here you keep a tiny note per row: for each field, the version at which it last changed. An update conflicts only if a field it wants to change has a note newer than the version the client read. If nothing conflicts, apply the non-null fields, add one to the version, and write the new version into the notes of the fields you changed. Use records with `with` expressions to produce the updated row.
explanation.junior: In EF Core this is the difference between a `[Timestamp]`/`RowVersion` concurrency token (whole-row) and a property-level check you implement yourself when `DbUpdateConcurrencyException` fires by comparing original, current and database values. Keep two dictionaries keyed by Id: the current `Row` and a per-field 'changed at' map; both lookups are O(1), so the whole run is O(rows + updates). Rules the tests pin down: an update is all-or-nothing (a partial conflict applies nothing); a client that read a version older than the row's initial version conflicts on every field because there is no history to prove otherwise, which is the safe default; `ExpectedVersion` newer than the row is a client bug and is reported differently from a conflict; an empty patch must not bump the version. Returning `rows.Select(r => current[r.Id])` preserves input order, since the harness compares lists positionally.
